claims.text: The baseline material is as-cast HfMoTaTiZr.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has a density of approximately 10.21 g/cm³.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has a room-temperature yield strength of approximately 1600 MPa.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has a yield strength of approximately 855 MPa at about 1000 °C.
Partially replacing Hf with V or another lighter element will reduce the alloy's density.
The proposed substitution will preserve a homogeneous BCC or related solid-solution phase.
Atomic-size differences in BCC high-entropy-alloy solid solutions produce lattice distortion that causes solid-solution strengthening.
After partial Hf substitution, the modified HfMoTaTiZr alloy will retain enough lattice distortion to maintain solid-solution strengthening.
The modified elemental distribution will avoid drastic changes in phase constitution.
Composition changes can induce secondary phases and associated changes in mechanical properties.
A modified alloy will retain room-temperature yield strength near 1600 MPa.
A modified alloy will retain yield strength near 855 MPa at approximately 1000 °C.
A modified alloy will retain ductility similar to the as-cast baseline.
Mechanical properties should be tested at 298 K and approximately 1273 K.
Modified and baseline alloys should be compared under equivalent tensile or compressive loading conditions.
A series replacing 10%, 20%, and 30% of the Hf should be prepared under the same as-cast conditions as the baseline.
The hypothesis is rejected if a modified alloy exhibits a statistically significant reduction greater than 10% in yield strength or ductility at either test temperature.

contradictions.description: The intervention is not compositionally consistent: it alternates between replacing Hf with V and increasing the Zr/V ratio. The baseline contains no V, and increasing Zr/V would normally mean increasing Zr relative to V rather than uniquely defining replacement of Hf by V.

The prediction is existential—an alloy variant is expected to retain performance—but the rejection rule says failure of any member of the 10%, 20%, and 30% series falsifies the hypothesis. Thus, one unsuccessful level would reject the hypothesis even if another level achieved the predicted outcome.
